## What the curve leaves out {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The options left off, and the specifications that nobody ran.** The review of the menu moved pooled OLS, random effects, the restricted samples and the weights off the curve, and the curve holds no person-level model, although two of the five reanalysts fitted one, and no lagged predictor, which nobody ran. The curve looks just as complete either way
- **The dependence.** All `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")` use the same 270 country-years, so they share their noise, and the width of the cloud cannot be read as `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")` independent results
- **Estimand drift.** Some of these specifications answer subtly different questions. The chart puts them on one axis; that does not make them commensurable
- **The data-building choices.** Everything upstream of the panel that the menu does not offer – which waves were pooled and to which years they were assigned, how the German and British samples were merged – is fixed for everyone here
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A curve is a **map of the menu you wrote**, and it cannot show whether that menu was the right one.
:::

::: notes
Four things are missing from the curve, and a chart as tidy as ours makes it easy to believe that it is complete. Some options were left off on purpose, because the review of the menu judged that they answer another question or answer this one less well, and the decision map gives the reason for each, while others are missing because nobody ran them, and the curve looks just as complete either way. All eight hundred and sixty-four specifications share the same two hundred and seventy country-years and therefore their noise, some of them answer subtly different questions, and everything upstream of the panel is fixed for everyone in this class. [advance] A curve maps the menu that you wrote, and it cannot show whether that menu was the right one.
:::

## Description and inference {#two-jobs-one-curve}

::: {.none}
**Description** – map how the estimate moves across every defensible choice. *(What our curve does.)*

::: {.fragment}
**Inference** – ask whether the curve *as a whole* is surprising if there were no effect at all. *(A different, harder job.)*
:::

::: {.fragment}
The two are detachable, and most published curves stop at description.
:::
:::

::: {.src}
@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse; @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis
:::

::: notes
A curve like ours does two different jobs. The first is description, showing how the estimate moves as the choices move, which is what we built and is useful on its own. [advance] The second is inference, which asks whether the curve as a whole is more extreme than we would expect if there were no effect at all. [advance] The two questions need different machinery and come apart cleanly: the robustness study did the description without the inference, and so far we have done the same. The next three slides concern what the second job takes.
:::

## Dependence among the estimates {#estimates-are-not-840-tests}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Every specification re-uses the **same 270 country-years**. The estimates are deeply dependent.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
'`r fmt_pct(share_sig(spec_curve))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05' **describes** the curve. It is not a p-value for the claim. Clustered errors allow for the years of one country resembling each other within each fit; they do not make the fits independent of one another.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Vote-counting across dependent specifications has no null distribution, so a tally of significant results is not evidence for the claim on its own.
:::
::::

::: notes
[advance] All eight hundred and sixty-four specifications use the same two hundred and seventy country-years. [advance] Seventy-seven per cent of them lie below zero with a CR2 p under point zero five, and it is tempting to read that share as the strength of the evidence, since most of the tests pass. The clustered errors already allow for the resemblance among the years of one country within each fit, but the specifications share the data and therefore the noise, so that sampling luck that pushed a handful of country-years the way of the claim pushed hundreds of specifications with them. The percentage describes the curve and is not a test of the claim. [advance] A tally of significant results across dependent specifications has no null distribution, and a test of the claim at the level of the curve needs to know what the whole curve would look like if there were nothing to find, a null that has to be constructed.
:::

## The permutation design {#building-the-nothing-the-permutation-design}

::: {.small}
- Break the one link that the claim needs: **shuffle each country's unemployment series in time** (jointly with growth), keeping everything else intact
- Refit **every specification on the curve** on each shuffled dataset, and repeat **B = 500** times
- Compare the observed curve to the 500 null curves: is ours more extreme than chance produces?
:::

::: {.src}
The design is worked through in your inference reading; permutation inference after @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues.
:::

::: notes
The claim says that the unemployment of a country moves its EU framing over time. To build the null, the unemployment series of each country is shuffled in time, together with growth, so that the macro side stays internally coherent, while the framing data stay untouched. In a shuffled panel the alignment between unemployment and framing is broken by construction, so any curve obtained from it is what chance alone produces on these data with these specifications. Done five hundred times, with the entire curve refitted each time, this gives five hundred null curves against which to compare ours. If our curve falls in the far tail of those null curves, the curve as a whole is evidence, and if it falls comfortably among them, the description stands and the inference does not.
:::

## Reading a curve-level test {#how-to-read-a-curve-level-test .smaller}

::: {.small}
- With B = 500, the smallest reportable p is **2/(B+1) ≈ 0.004**, a floor set by the number of draws, not a zero
- Near p = .05 the Monte-Carlo error is about **±0.01**, so treat p = .04 and p = .06 as the same finding
- [A DESIGN, NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – a curve-level test has to be fully specified before anyone runs it, and this one has not been run; today we read the design only
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Discussion:** the cosmopolitan scale on the curve has `r nrow(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, outcome == "mcosmo"))` specifications: **`r fmt_pct(share_below(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, outcome == "mcosmo")))` below zero, `r fmt_pct(share_sig(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, outcome == "mcosmo")))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05.** Strong evidence? *Against what null?*
:::

::: notes
Two points about reading such a test come before the discussion. With five hundred draws, the smallest p-value that the test can report is two over five hundred and one, about point zero zero four, a floor set by the number of draws rather than a zero, which more draws lower at a real cost in computing time. Near the boundary of point zero five the Monte Carlo error is around plus or minus point zero one, so a permutation p of point zero four and one of point zero six count as the same finding. The badge says that this test is designed and has not been run, so what you read today is a plan whose result nobody yet knows, which is the position that a preregistration puts you in. [advance] For the cosmopolitan scale alone, the outcome instructed by the robustness study, the curve holds two hundred and eighty-eight specifications, ninety-four per cent below zero and sixty-six per cent below zero with a CR2 p under point zero five. Is that strong evidence, and against what null? [take answers; the answer sought: we cannot say until we know what chance produces on these dependent data]
:::

## What stands without the test

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Everything descriptive survives: the share that the **estimator** carries, the placement of the reference results, where the sign changes come from, **your dot**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Only one sentence depends on the permutation test: "the curve as a whole is unlikely under no effect".
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Careful reporting says which of the two layers a claim belongs to.
:::
::::

::: notes
Most of what the curve has shown needs no permutation at all. [advance] The share carried by the estimator is a description and stands, as do the places of the six reference results once each is converted on its own degrees of freedom, the origin of the sign changes in pooled OLS and in the samples without the bailout countries, and your own dot, with the whole structure of the curve. [advance] The single sentence that has to wait for the test is that the curve as a whole is unlikely if there is no effect. [advance] Keeping these two layers apart in your own writing, and saying to which of them a claim belongs, is what literacy about inference means in practice.
:::
